articles.title_orig: Air Astana, China Southern Form Kazakhstan-China JV
articles.title_zh: Air Astana, China Southern Form Kazakhstan-China JV
articles.content_orig:
Air Astana and China Southern Airlines have signed a joint venture (JV) agreement covering flights between Kazakhstan and China, deepening a relationship that already includes codesharing.
The airlines plan to coordinate schedules, expand their codeshare arrangements and undertake joint marketing. They say closer cooperation will give passengers more flight options, smoother transfers and wider access to destinations across their respective networks.
“China is a strategically important market for Air Astana, and Kazakhstan is well positioned as a gateway connecting Europe and Asia,” Air Astana Vice President for Partnerships and Alliances Richard Ledger says.
The agreement builds on a codeshare partnership announced in June covering 10 routes. Air Astana-operated services included in that arrangement connect Almaty with Beijing Capital, Guangzhou and Urumqi, as well as Astana with Beijing.
China Southern’s codeshare routes include flights to Almaty from Beijing Daxing, Guangzhou, Urumqi and Xi’an, alongside services to Astana from Guangzhou and Urumqi.
The JV comes as travel between Kazakhstan and China grows rapidly. OAG Schedules Analyser data shows airlines are scheduled to offer approximately 862,500 two-way seats during winter 2026-27, up 52.1% from about 567,100 a year earlier. The number of nonstop airport pairs increases from 18 to 22, while scheduled flight sectors rise 51.8% to more than 4,900.
China Southern remains the largest operator in the market, offering approximately 226,900 seats during the season, up 1.1% year over year. Air Astana ranks second with about 204,900 seats, more than double its winter 2025-26 capacity.
Together, the JV partners account for just over half of all scheduled seats. However, their combined share is down from 57.2% a year earlier as rival airlines expand more quickly.
Air China’s capacity increases 112.9% to approximately 136,600 seats, while Air Astana Group subsidiary FlyArystan grows 275% to 132,300. Kazakhstan’s SCAT Airlines offers about 89,000 seats, up 26.6%.
Air Astana and China Southern overlap directly on only two airport pairs in the current winter schedule: Almaty-Urumqi and Almaty-Guangzhou. The rest of their networks are largely complementary, with the two airlines collectively serving 10 nonstop airport pairs between the countries.
The expansion follows an agreement between the Kazakh and Chinese governments in July to raise the bilateral allowance for scheduled passenger flights by 22.6%, from 124 to 152 per week. The number of Chinese destinations available to airlines serving Kazakhstan was also increased to 11 through the addition of Chongqing.

articles.title_orig: Xi tells German president China and EU must ‘stay anchored to their partnership’
articles.title_zh: Xi tells German president China and EU must ‘stay anchored to their partnership’
articles.content_orig:
Frank-Walter Steinmeier was visiting Beijing at a time of heightened concern in Brussels over the widening trade gap
China and the European Union can resolve their differences through dialogue, Chinese President Xi Jinping told his German counterpart Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Friday.
“China has always regarded the European Union as a partner,” Xi said, according to state broadcaster CCTV, adding that cooperation between the two sides outweighed competition.
“As long as [both sides] stay anchored to their partnership and engage in dialogue on an equal footing, differences and challenges can always be resolved and will not stand in the way of China-EU relations moving forward,” the Chinese leader said.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls more than 2% as investors rotate out of tech after Amazon, Intel earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls more than 2% as investors rotate out of tech after Amazon, Intel earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 610 points, or 2.3%, in early trading on Friday after disappointing earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel renewed fears about the prospects for artificial intelligence.
Intel's stock plunged nearly 29% once trading opened, while Alphabet shares continued to wobble after the company's Class A stock slid more than 12% on Thursday, its worst day since the company went public as Google in 2004.
"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.
The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped 1.2% and 0.4%, respectively, after the opening bell.
The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.
Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."
"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
articles.title_zh: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
articles.content_orig:
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

articles.title_orig: Gold drops below $4,000, silver tumbles as Hormuz attack lifts oil prices - Kitco AM Report
articles.title_zh: Gold drops below $4,000, silver tumbles as Hormuz attack lifts oil prices - Kitco AM Report
articles.content_orig:
Articles by Kitco News Wire were generated by Kitco's AI-assisted reporting workflow and reviewed by Kitco News editorial staff, with every claim independently verified before publication.
Kitco labels all AI-assisted content as part of our commitment to editorial transparency.
For questions or corrections, contact the Kitco News editorial team.
(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in early U.S. trading Friday, as renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz pushed crude oil prices higher and reinforced inflation concerns despite fresh evidence of moderating U.S. wage growth. Precious metals remained under selling pressure following Thursday's declines, with gold slipping below $4,000.00 an ounce and silver falling to its lowest levels of the year. Spot gold was trading near $3,958.80 an ounce, down $61.34, or 1.32%, while spot silver was trading near $50.080, down $2.120, or 4,06%. Gold was heading toward a second consecutive monthly decline, while silver continued to underperform amid concerns about industrial demand and restrictive monetary policy.
The latest U.S. employment cost figures provided some evidence that labor-related inflation pressure is moderating, although wage growth remains elevated. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. Wages and salaries increased 0.7%, compared with 0.9% in the previous quarter, while benefit costs rose 0.9%, down from 1.0%. Total compensation costs increased 3.4% from a year earlier, unchanged from the annual rate recorded in June, while wages and salaries rose 3.1% and benefit costs increased 3.9%. The slowdown in quarterly wage growth provides some relief from concerns about persistent labor-cost inflation, although annual compensation growth remains above levels consistent with the Federal Reserve's longer-term inflation objective.
The employment report followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product figures and another increase in the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge. The U.S. economy expanded at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter , accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter, supported by resilient consumer spending and business investment. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation increased 0.5% on the month and 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation rose 0.3% and 3.1%, respectively. The combination of accelerating economic growth and persistent underlying inflation continues to complicate the case for easier monetary policy, even as Friday's wage figures suggest some moderation in labor costs.
Market positioning remains focused on the possibility of another Federal Reserve interest rate increase in December following Wednesday's decision to leave the benchmark federal funds target range unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%. The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to maintain rates , with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Futures markets assigned approximately an 83% probability to a December increase following Thursday's GDP and inflation releases , with the latest wage data providing some counterweight to those expectations. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield declined 7 basis points Thursday to approximately 4.98%, as weakness in major technology shares encouraged demand for government bonds. However, gold continued to fall despite lower yields, reflecting the influence of persistent inflation concerns, expectations for further tightening and broader precious metals liquidation.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation deteriorated further Friday following another attack on a commercial tanker in the strategic waterway, highlighting the continuing risks to Middle Eastern energy supplies. Maritime security authorities confirmed that a tanker was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, although responsibility for the incident had not been established. The attack came amid persistent threats to regional shipping and uncertainty about the prospects for renewed negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Diplomatic initiatives involving Qatar and other regional mediators have yet to produce an agreement, while disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the broader conflict continue to prevent a lasting settlement.
Crude oil prices rose sharply following the latest attack, with December Brent futures climbing toward $117.15 a barrel and WTI advancing to approximately $103.79. Brent was heading toward a monthly gain of approximately 13%, while WTI was on course for an increase of around 15%, reflecting sustained concerns about Gulf energy supplies and the possibility of further military escalation. The risk of renewed confrontation has become particularly important ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, with uncertainty surrounding the next phase of U.S.-Iran relations adding to the geopolitical premium embedded in crude prices. Although alternative export routes have helped mitigate some of the disruption to Gulf petroleum shipments, continued tanker attacks and elevated maritime security costs remain significant obstacles to restoring normal commercial flows through Hormuz.
For gold, the continuing confrontation supports defensive demand, but the inflationary consequences of elevated crude oil prices have reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve may need to maintain restrictive monetary policy for longer. The metal's continued decline despite geopolitical instability and lower Treasury yields suggests that liquidation pressure and the interest rate outlook remain dominant influences on near-term price action. Silver has suffered significantly greater losses as the broader precious metals decline coincides with concerns about industrial demand, elevated energy costs and restrictive borrowing conditions. Its break below previously established technical support has added to selling pressure, leaving the metal increasingly vulnerable to further liquidation.
Global equity markets were weaker before the U.S. open as disappointing corporate earnings and renewed concerns about artificial intelligence investment weighed on technology shares. S&P 500 futures declined approximately 1.0%, while Nasdaq futures dropped 2.3% and Dow futures were little changed. Alphabet's sharp decline Thursday was followed by additional pressure on major technology companies after cautious earnings guidance from Amazon and Intel. European equity markets were mixed, while Asian markets were mostly lower as investors assessed corporate earnings, higher energy prices and the outlook for global monetary policy. The combination of rising crude prices, elevated financing costs and uncertainty surrounding large-scale artificial intelligence investment continued to undermine risk appetite, although the resulting demand for government bonds provided limited support for precious metals.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil prices higher and trading near $103.79 a barrel, while December Brent crude futures were near $117.15, reflecting renewed concerns about Gulf energy supplies. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note was trading near the 5.0% area following Thursday's decline. The U.S. dollar remained comparatively firm, while persistent expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening and elevated energy prices continued to limit gold's ability to benefit from geopolitical uncertainty. ( Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq set for sharp drop as Amazon, Intel amplify AI spending worries
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq set for sharp drop as Amazon, Intel amplify AI spending worries
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) shares were slammed following the company's third-quarter earnings report, as its search revenue growth slowed and it missed expectations. However, this problem looks fixable, and the company's cloud computing business delivered exceptional results.
Let's take a closer look at the search giant's Q3 results and why I think the stock is a buy on this dip.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
The biggest reason Alphabet shares sank was that its search revenue growth decelerated from 17% from the second quarter and missed expectations. For Q3, search revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion, below analyst estimates of $64.96 billion. The slower growth stemmed from a combination of currency fluctuations, the timing of the World Cup, the end of the European Union de minimis exception (no duties on low-cost items), and lower monetization of AI queries compared with traditional search.
While the company said currency was the biggest drag, the last one is what caught everyone's attention. Alphabet said it saw its highest query growth in five years, but revenue growth still slowed. This means it was seeing lower revenue per search with its newer AI queries. The worry is that this could become a structural issue. However, this looks fixable as it works to find the right ad formats. The company will start offering ads in AI international markets for the first time, while also introducing new multi-turn ads (ads that adapt to evolving content during AI queries) in the U.S.
Management also spoke positively about Alphabet's stand-alone Gemini app, which recently reached 1 billion users. It said it was the fastest-growing product in its history. The company also launched its new Carbon model the same day as its earnings report, shortly after introducing its Argon model.
While Alphabet's search segment was a disappointment, its cloud computing unit was a huge bright spot. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, and topped the $28.7 billion cloud revenue consensus. The company's cloud growth is far outpacing that of rivals Microsoft and Amazon as it takes market share. Impressively, cloud operating income more than tripled to $11.1 billion, as its operating margins climbed from 23.7% a year ago to 36.2%. Cloud computing is a high-fixed-cost business, and Alphabet is seeing significant operating leverage. As such, expect its cloud computing operating income to continue to outpace revenue growth.
Alphabet ended the quarter with a backlog of $561 billion. It expects about 55% of that to convert to revenue over the next two years. This also includes sales of tensor processing units (TPUs).
Looking at Alphabet's other segments, YouTube ad revenue climbed 9% to $11.2 billion, while Google Network revenue edged up 1% to $7.5 billion. Subscription (YouTube Premium and Music) revenue, meanwhile, rose 11% to $14.3 billion.
Overall, Alphabet's Q3 revenue jumped 25% to $127.6 billion, while its earnings per share fell 26% to $2.12. Much of this was due to a paper loss on its SpaceX investment, and adjusted EPS was around $2.67. However, the results still missed analyst expectations for EPS of $3.02 on revenue of $128.2 billion
Also notable during the quarter was Alphabet's negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion as it ramped up its AI infrastructure spending. That was also below the negative $2.7 billion analysts expected, but it did include a $5.2 billion fine. Operating cash flow, meanwhile, was a robust $42.3 billion for the quarter.
Following the stock's dip, Alphabet trades at a forward P/E of just above 18.5 times 2027 analyst estimates. That ultimately should prove to be a bargain for a company with the most complete tech stack.
Google Cloud has become a monster, with rapid revenue growth and great operating leverage, and its TPUs give the company a distinct advantage and additional underappreciated growth driver. Meanwhile, Alphabet is seeing strong query growth, but it needs to find a way to better monetize AI Mode searches, which should be fixable.
In typical Wall Street fashion, investors are shooting first and asking questions later, creating a great opportunity to buy this top AI stock on this dip.

articles.title_orig: The Apple Pencil turned the Duo into my new favorite notebook
articles.title_zh: The Apple Pencil turned the Duo into my new favorite notebook
articles.content_orig:
Ignore the pile of previous favorite notebooks; this is the one that’s gonna change it all for me.
Ignore the pile of previous favorite notebooks; this is the one that’s gonna change it all for me.
Apple’s $2,000 folding phone is a surprisingly good stand-in for a $20 notebook.
Believe me; nothing gets me going quite like a new notebook. This one will be different, I think. This time, I really will take it everywhere. Inspiration can strike at any moment, and you have to be ready, says David Sedaris in that one MasterClass I watched on a flight. With this one special new notebook, I will see the world differently. I’ll steal moments for myself to write, rather than pulling out my phone to scroll at every opportunity like a trained monkey. And a few weeks, a month, or maybe a year later, I’ll concede that it didn’t change everything and add it to my notebook graveyard. At least they all look nice on the corner of my desk?
The iPhone Duo is not a notebook — although it is the first iPhone to support the Apple Pencil. Even so, I can see the new notebook effect in the eyes of the people I talk to about the Duo. “Is that the new iPhone?” the conversation starts. I hand over the phone and give them the short version of our 26-minute review : It’s nice, it’s kind of heavy and chunky, you should wait for the second generation. They nod, but I can tell they still want one anyway. They’re tired of their big/aging/boring phone, they tell me. And this one would be different.
It’s hard to argue against. It really is a different phone. Its new form factor lets you actually use it in meaningfully different ways. The Duo can act like a vintage Hasselblad with a waist-level viewfinder. It can be a book-shaped e-reader. And with this week’s iOS 27.2 update officially adding that Apple Pencil support, it can also be a notebook.
Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something.
That’s the USB-C Apple Pencil, to be specific, so there’s no pressure sensitivity. You do still get the ability to “scribble” handwriting that’s automatically turned into text in apps like Messages or Safari, as you can on the iPad. But even with the basic stylus, there’s a lot of fun to be had doodling and writing notes out by hand. I asked for some Pencil-friendly app suggestions and downloaded a handful. I used the native Notes app to scribble down some article ideas. I set my five-year-old loose on a blank note, to his delight (the phone survived the encounter, too). But having the stylus in my hand led me on an unexpected side quest: turning the whole phone into a notebook.
Why not? It’s notebook-shaped. Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something. Maybe I could cajole the Duo into being something less distracting, more input-friendly. I put together a minimalist home and lockscreen designed around this theory. I won’t lie, it’s pretty nice. But I don’t think I curated my way out of the new-notebook trap, even if it was a fun exercise.
There aren’t many apps ready to take advantage of the new stylus support. Notes, unsurprisingly, is where the Pencil is at its best. When you use the Pencil for handwriting in the app, you can enable the auto-refine handwriting feature that neatens up your writing while still keeping its unique characteristics intact. This has been available on the iPad since 2024 , and it’s particularly useful on the Duo’s comparatively small screens.
It occasionally gets tripped up by some of my scrawl that it either doesn’t know what to do with or misinterprets — it kept insisting on turning a “u” into an “o” in one instance. And it works after a small delay when you pause your writing, which I can see being distracting if I really want to get into a flow state. But it’s a nice middle ground between my untidy scribbles and full handwriting-to-text conversion and very handy for something like a grocery list.
The Notes app also has a big homescreen widget that kind of turned the phone into a notebook, but wasn’t nice to look at. After some more digging , I found almost exactly what I’d been looking for: TypeDraw .
It’s a $4.99 one-time purchase, and it’s optimized for the Duo. When you launch the app, it turns the cover screen into the front of your notebook. To flip to a page, you can either swipe on the cover screen or open the whole phone. It’s a delight.
TypeDraw isn’t really for power note-takers the way other apps like Bear are . You can’t add tags or links between notes, and you’re limited to one notebook. But it automatically creates a table of contents at the beginning based on the headings of your notes, so you can skip right to the section you’re looking for. Plus, if you drag your finger along the “elastic” on the cover, it’ll stretch and snap back, complete with satisfying haptics. I have zero regrets about the five bucks I spent on this app.
Using the Apple Pencil with the Duo gave me one more reason to love the matte finish on the inner screen. There’s just a bit of resistance moving the pencil across the display that feels more satisfying than the lifeless plastic-on-glass effect of writing on the cover screen. It’s not going to feel like using a Remarkable tablet or anything, but it’s nice.
The Pencil has one other neat trick — it can stick to the Duo’s hinge magnetically when the phone is closed. The pencil is longer than the phone, so it’s an awkward fit, but it’s been a handy way to carry both around the house as I relocate throughout the day.
I was only, like, 60 percent serious when I set out to turn the Duo into a notebook, but I actually liked the idea the more I got into it. Reimagining my homescreen around creating rather than consuming feels like a worthwhile cause, and I’m planning to live with it for a while to see if it inspires any changes in my phone habits. To that end, I also set up a shortcut to launch TypeDraw whenever I open the inner screen.
But I think the most useful part of this exercise was examining, once again, how much stuff I really need on my homescreen. I can get most things done with a Spotlight Search or a tap in the Control Center. Siri is much more helpful now too, and it’s always lurking nearby to help out. The grid of apps I’m so used to is mostly for emotional support at this point. I didn’t need a folding phone to learn that, but it helped.
Above all, the new-notebook effect proved to be just as strong as always. The shiny new thing eventually fades into the background. You certainly don’t need a $2,000 phone to reevaluate your homescreen. You can — and I will continue to — just carry a little notebook around with your regular phone. A fun new gadget is delightful, don’t get me wrong. But don’t hang all your hopes and dreams for a new you on one of them.
Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

articles.title_orig: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times .
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia said their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed and the White House for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed told the paper its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

Ukrainian president says Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position strongest ⁠in some ​time. What we know on day 1,708
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukrainian forces are retaking territory through a series of offensives , adding Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position was the strongest it had been ⁠in some ​time. The Ukrainian president, citing ⁠a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in ⁠eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in ​key areas.
The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian president Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine. The call by Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to ⁠influence the diplomatic process after US president Donald ⁠Trump stunned allies by agreeing to buy Russian diesel, plunging ties with Ukraine to their lowest point in 18 months.
While a localised ceasefire appears to holding in Ukraine’s south, Russian strikes damaged a university campus and Kyiv’s important Southern Bridge overnight , in what Zelenskyy described as “a serious escalation” against ​Ukrainian logistics. A Ukrainian military source told Reuters that Russia ‌had hit the bridge with four Iskander ​ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy said energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure in ​10 other regions had also been attacked overnight.
Kyiv plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias ($22 ⁠million) to build water crossings over the River Dnipro that divides ⁠the capital into two ⁠parts , ​the city’s mayor has said, as Russia escalates its attacks on ⁠bridges.
Romanian president Nicusor Dan has called an alleged Russian sabotage plot last month a “grave violation” of the Nato member’s sovereignty and security . Dan’s remarks on Tuesday came a day after the Romanian intelligence service said it identified a Russia-coordinated “sabotage network” linked to a fire in central Brasov County last month, which damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three foreign nationals – two Belarusians and one Ukrainian, all residing in EU countries – were being investigated in connection with the fire. Romania’s foreign ministry said on Tuesday it had summoned Russia’s ambassador in Bucharest. The Russian embassy in Romania said its ambassador rejected the “baseless” accusations.
France has temporarily relocated a maritime patrol aircraft to ⁠Romania to help identify navigation dangers and bolster the protection of critical energy infrastructure ⁠in the Black ⁠Sea. At least eight cargo ships have been hit ⁠near the coast Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, ⁠with about 34 sailors reported dead or missing. Romania’s defence ministry said on Tuesday the purpose is “to identify dangers to navigation and increase the ability to protect critical infrastructure in Romania’s exclusive ⁠economic zone”.
Poland will host a maintenance centre for the US-made Patriot air-defence system. The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the US, deputy defence minister Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on social media. Poland, a Nato member bordering Ukraine, serves as a major logistics hub for military aid sent by Kyiv’s allies. Patriot interceptor missiles are regarded as among Ukraine’s most important air-defence assets as it seeks to repel escalating Russian missile and drone attacks.
Pope Leo XIV’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit the capital, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a ceasefire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during a phone calls with Putin and Zelenskyy.

articles.title_orig: Earnings live updates: Exxon, Chevron refining margins jump, lifting earnings

Oops, something went wrong
Third quarter earnings season was in full swing this week, with corporate results dropping from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals were represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also opened their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
ExxonMobil ( XOM ) reported third-quarter income that topped expectations on Friday, as the oil major was bolstered by a jump in refining margins triggered by ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Adjusted earnings per share stood at $4.23 for the period, topping Bloomberg consensus estimates of $4.13.
Twin conflicts — the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine — have disrupted activity at critical fuel-producing facilities, causing prices to spike.
In preliminary earnings earlier this month, ExxonMobil said higher refining margins would add around $4.5 billion to its overall results, following a boost of $4.1 billion in the preceding quarter. The returns echoed similarly solid profits at other Western oil groups, such as Shell and TotalEnergies.
Chevron Corporation ( CVX ) shares are up in premarket trading after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped expectations.
Adjusted earnings were $5.28 per share, surpassing analyst estimates of $4.88, as the energy giant benefited from stronger refining margins and higher crude oil prices. Revenue reached $67.8 billion, exceeding the $60.55 billion consensus estimate and up 36% from $49.7 billion in the same quarter last year.
Chevron stock rose 1% before the bell on Friday.
The company posted adjusted earnings of $10.4 billion for the quarter, compared to $3.6 billion in the prior-year period. U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput of 1.09 million barrels per day with utilization rates near 98%, while downstream operations delivered significantly higher margins on refined product sales. Shares rose 2.2% following the results.
Reddit ( RDDT ) stock plunged 17% after hours. The company reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings and revenue, but investors were disappointed by softer-than-expected US daily active users and a subdued fourth quarter outlook.

Global daily active users (DAUs): increased 12% year over year to 130.3 million
US daily active users: decreased 2% year over year to 50.7 million

Amazon ( AMZN ) reported third quarter results Thursday, missing on the top and bottom lines, sending the stock falling.
Follow live updates from the report and earnings call here >
Starbucks ( SBUX ) earnings beat expectations on Thursday, as the company looked to move beyond its turnaround plan to accelerate growth.
For the fifth consecutive quarter, the coffee giant posted better-than-expected same-store sales growth, up 7.2%, compared to Wall Street's expectations of 6.2%. That was driven by US sales, which were up 7.7%, with roughly a 5% increase in ticket sizes as customers spent more at Starbucks and roughly a 2% increase in transactions.
"We have a clear plan. We've been working the plan. And the plan is working," CEO Brian Niccol said in prepared remarks. He added that the company is "operating with greater consistency" and that more customers are going to Starbucks.
Adjusted earnings came in at $0.80, more than the $0.71 Wall Street forecast. Revenue fell short, at $9.1 billion, compared with the $9.2 billion the Street was looking for, reflecting the sale of Starbucks China business.
International sales fell short of Wall Street's expectations, rising just 0.9% compared to the roughly 3% growth the Street was looking for.
Intel ( INTC ) reported better-than-anticipated third-quarter earnings after the bell Thursday, but Q4 revenue outlook fell short of Wall Street's expectations on declining PC sales.
Intel stock fell more than 20% on the news.
In the fourth quarter, Intel is projecting revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the $17 billion analysts expected.
Intel says the shortfall is a result of a worse-than-anticipated drop in PC revenue. The industry is contending with two overlapping factors at the moment: difficult comparisons to last year, when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, forcing enterprises around the world to purchase newer Windows 11 systems, and the steady increase in PC prices, which is eating into demand.
Rivian ( RIVN ) reported upbeat third quarter results after the bell on Thursday and boosted its guidance, citing strong R2 sales.
Rivian reported Q3 revenue of $2.155 billion vs. $2.02 billion per Bloomberg consensus, up 38% from a year ago. Rivian posted an adjusted loss per share of $0.48 vs. $0.61, and an adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) loss of $435 million vs. $575.9 million, narrower than the $602 million loss from last year.
Rivian also reported a gross profit of $176 million, up $152 million from a quarter ago, though the automotive segment remained negative.
Rivian stock gained on the news.
Sandisk ( SNDK ) stock climbed in extended trading after solid across-the-board earnings and guidance beats.
Notably, Sandisk announced it will enact an eight-for-one stock split, effective Nov. 19.
Here's what Sandisk reported, compared to analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue : $11 billion, versus $10.7 billion expected
Earnings per share: $52.60, versus $47.15 expected
Fiscal second quarter revenue guidance: $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion, with a midpoint above the $12.23 billion forecast by Wall Street analysts
Fiscal second quarter adjusted earnings guidance: $55.00 to $57.00 (on a pre-split basis), with a midpoint above the Street's $53.30 forecast
The NAND flash memory maker has been a key beneficiary of the AI data center boom.
"We have started fiscal year 2027 with another quarter of strong performance, with robust and growing demand for our products driving outpaced growth in our data center business," CEO David Goeckeler said in a press release.
The stock has soared in 2026, but it's had a rocky few months as of late. Year to date, shares are up over 460%, but the stock has largely treaded water since July.
Crocs ( CROX ) stock soared 25% on Thursday to its highest price in over two years as investors cheered on a return to growth for the footwear company's HeyDude loafer brand and a brighter outlook for 2026 sales.
In the third quarter, HeyDude revenue increased 6.1% over the previous year to $170 million, marking the first sales increase in six quarters for the struggling shoe brand.
Crocs bought HeyDude for $2.5 billion in 2022, its largest acquisition ever. But the brand struggled amid excess inventory and discounting, causing investors to become fed up with lagging sales.
HeyDude makes up roughly 16% of Crocs' total revenue, while the flagship Crocs brand accounts for the remaining 84% of sales.

Tensions in the Middle East are escalating again as a tanker was reported on fire after explosive devices were attached to its hull while the vessel was attempting to transit outbound in the Strait of Hormuz.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which is affiliated with the Royal Navy, said in a warning notice that it had received a third report on Thursday that a tanker transiting outbound was on fire 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, in the Strait of Hormuz.
In a subsequent update, UKMTO said it had received “a verified report confirming the crew is safe, and there is no environmental impact.”
According to this report, the tanker was approached on the port side by a small boat which attached two explosive devices to the hull above the waterline.
“The subsequent blasts resulted in a fire in the engine room which temporarily disabled the vessel. The fire is now reported as extinguished and the vessel is continuing to its next port of call,” UKMTO said.
Separately, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Thursday that four tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and disputed the U.S. Central Command’s claim that U.S. forces had cleared the primary transit routes of mines.
“The reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the air, on land and at sea, not on social media and in America’s media war rooms,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said, as quoted by CNBC.
The renewed tensions and the continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure sent oil prices rising again early on Friday.
Oil is on track for its fourth consecutive monthly gain, with Brent Crude prices hitting $117 per barrel in Asian trade amid market concerns and fears that an escalation in Iran is imminent following the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.

articles.title_orig: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.title_zh: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.content_orig:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.
The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.
Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking , are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.
Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.
The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.
Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.
"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.
"We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.
At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.
Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.
An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.
It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.
Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.
Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".
The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."
Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".
Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.
Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.
Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.
In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office , in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.
Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.

articles.title_orig: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.title_zh: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.content_orig:
The brutal business of selling mirrors is not for the faint-hearted. The challenge is category differentiation, given that a mirror has one simple task—reflection. One of Greg Jackson’s first jobs was working for a mirror manufacturer which, at best, broke even or made a small profit. And then he had an idea.
“We started making mirrors that had really wide frames,” the founder of Octopus Energy (the U.K.’s largest energy provider) told me. “And on a picture [on the internet], suddenly we had a mirror that looked different from everybody else’s. And they sold like hotcakes – and that transformed the business.”
Approaching a business from a different point of view is an essential ingredient in the hunt for innovation. Jackson’s essential insight when it came to mirrors was that, online, every product looked the same. That is what the customer saw. And he realized that if the customer saw something different (a mirror with a wide frame), they might buy it. Which they did.
Not seeing something that is obvious to an outsider is a firm’s “incumbency cost”— embedded in the regular behavior of doing the same thing tomorrow as you did yesterday. It is one of the most significant brakes on the ability to grow.
“I think the single biggest factor affecting Europe—and an issue the U.S. is not immune to—is incumbency,” he told me. “China and the Gulf are not held back by incumbent industries. Instead they are, at huge pace, delivering the new world. If I look at electric vehicles as an example, there’s not an incumbent car industry in China that’s struggling to manage the transition to an entirely new technology. But if I look at Europe, European governments and consumers want electric vehicles, but the European car companies have not yet been able to be competitive at building them.”
“If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need”
Chinese electric vehicle sales in Europe are growing rapidly. Chery has tripled sales in Europe in the past year, BYD has doubled, Geely is up a third, and SAIC is up 23%. Taking the four leading Chinese car makers together, their EV market share is now at 14.6%, up from 9.6%, according to the latest figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. In response to claims of state subsidized dumping by China, the European Union has applied duties of up to 35% on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Chinese cars are still over 20% cheaper to buy.
“Incumbents crowd out the innovators in many sectors and markets,” Jackson said. “It wasn’t the Post Office [the U.K.’s public mail service] that invented email. The music industry held back streaming and digital music for 10 to 20 years. What you need is routes to market for new technologies, and I think that can be a challenge in Europe because so many of the big industries essentially have a stranglehold on policy.
“Economists have said that nearly all productivity growth comes from new companies. If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need.”
Jackson said that Europe has a number of successful sectors that it can learn from—for example, the continent enjoys a vibrant and innovative fintech sector whereas in America “they take my card around the back of the bar because their terminals and processes are so dated.” Few people have seen a check in Europe in more than a decade.
Octopus grew out of the need for a new way to manage energy supply and demand. Jackson initially attempted to convince legacy businesses that they would be far more efficient with a fully overhauled technology platform but, after not progressing very far, decided that he could build a team that could modernize more quickly.
“The idea was that through technology, we would be able to provide lower costs because we’d be more operationally efficient,” he said. “We’d be more agile, so we can incorporate technologies like electric vehicles and solar panels and batteries directly into the energy system very efficiently. That would also help with cleaning up energy because you can use more renewables more cost-effectively if you’re more agile. We set out building that company in 2015, and nine years later, we became the biggest energy company in the UK, overtaking all the incumbents.
“We came from outside energy, we came from tech, and just like the people that built Uber didn’t come from personal transportation, and the people that built Airbnb didn’t come from hospitality, and the people that built Amazon didn’t own bookshops. What we were able to do is build an energy company not based around the assumptions of the industry, but using technology to meet the needs of customers.”
The brute force of market dynamics is pushing the world towards a different energy mix. In the European Union, wind and solar power produced more electricity than fossil fuels for the first time last year, according to Ember, the energy think tank.
“The technologies of electricity are improving exponentially, and the technologies of hydrocarbons are not,” Jackson said. “A car engine costs roughly the same now as it did 20 years ago. They’re not particularly more efficient. Meanwhile, an electric vehicle battery today costs 10 times less than it did 15 years ago. Solar panels cost 200 times less than they did 40 years ago. Wind turbines have come down two thirds in price over the last 20 years.”
Jackson was in China earlier in the year and said that electrification is continuing at pace, with battery swap stations, rather than recharging, reducing the amount of time drivers have to wait to between three and five minutes. “It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is. The drivers don’t care about the price of diesel.” Which might give Donald Trump pause for thought as he eyes both the American mid-term elections and the rising cost of fuel in the U.S.

articles.content_orig:
Training off Second Thomas and Sabina shoals tests small boats, surveillance drones and simulated vessel boardings amid ongoing spats
China’s coastguard has carried out an exercise featuring water cannons and drones near two disputed reefs at the centre of its simmering South China Sea contention with the Philippines to prepare for “foreign infringement”, according to state media.
A China Coast Guard flotilla “recently” conducted “comprehensive maritime law-enforcement training” in the waters around Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal, according to state broadcaster CCTV, which did not specify dates.
The official television network stated that the drill had focused on foreign vessels “illegally” entering the waters around the two shoals, while covering surveillance, tracking, maritime traffic control and tactical manoeuvres by small boats.
It also included practising water cannon use, drone operations and optoelectronic evidence collection – a technique that uses optical and electronic sensors to detect and record evidence that may not be visible to the naked eye – according to the report.

articles.title_orig: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
articles.title_zh: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance .
Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.
Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”
The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis . “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.
“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.
The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor . Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.
Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.
Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations —often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.
Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.
“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”
“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”
TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit , which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.
“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”
While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”
Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

articles.title_orig: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent the week punishing Big Tech's biggest AI spenders . Amazon ( AMZN ) just posted the deepest cash burn in its history.
Amazon's free cash flow — the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses, and equipment — was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September, according to its third quarter results released Thursday. That's nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.
One quarter did most of the damage. Amazon spent about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
So far, the spending is working.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) grew 39% to about $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon's operating margin of nearly 14% was its highest ever. CEO Andy Jassy said in the release that he projects AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) computing commitments alone amount to about a fifth of AWS's backlog as of June , according to Yahoo Finance calculations based on the AI lab's IPO filing.
Paying for it has meant borrowing. Amazon's long-term debt reached about $173 billion at the end of September, up from about $66 billion at the end of 2025, while its cash fell to about $56 billion from about $87 billion. Meta ( META ) took a different route this week with a nearly $100 billion stock sale .
Bond traders have noticed. The cost of insuring Amazon's debt against default for five years with credit default swaps has risen about 50% since early August, according to Bloomberg data. That price implies roughly a 7% chance of default over five years, up from about 5%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Amazon stock fell about 4% Thursday to its lowest close since July 30 as Alphabet's record drop weighed on Big Tech. It slid further after-hours as sales, earnings, and its profit outlook for the holiday quarter missed estimates.
Amazon isn't planning to ease off. CEO Andy Jassy said on the company's earnings call Thursday that Amazon still expects to spend about $220 billion this year, mostly on AWS, and to "spend meaningfully more in 2027."
"Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that's not the world that we live in," Jassy said. "We can fund this plan. I think it will forever change the size of Amazon."

articles.title_orig: Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
articles.title_zh: Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
articles.content_orig:
Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty game after an angry reaction from victims' families.
Real life news coverage of the 2022 disaster which killed almost 160 people was included in an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4 to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.
Bereaved families said they were "appalled" to see the footage - which included people being removed on stretchers, body bags on the street and resuscitation efforts - repurposed for the game.
Activision, which makes Call of Duty, has since apologised and confirmed it would be removed in the game's next update on 12 November.
The crush happened in the narrow alleys of Seoul's Itaewon district when more than 100,000 people went to the area to celebrate Halloween four years ago.
The streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.
In a statement on Thursday , the families of those who died said the disaster "was a tragedy that caused hundreds of casualties, and citizens who took part in the rescue or witnessed it have suffered from trauma until now".
"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used to create a scene in a game.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless."
Activision confirmed it had used real news coverage of the disaster "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insisted it had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
Confirming on Friday that the footage would be removed in a statement, the company offered its condolences and apologised to the bereaved families and victims who have been hurt by this incident.
The decision was welcomed by the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association, however the group told the BBC they had not received a direct apology from Activision.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told BBC Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".
Additional reporting by Sophie Jeong

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Qatar pushes for U.S.-Iran deal under shadow of Trump's threats to resume attacks
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Qatar pushes for U.S.-Iran deal under shadow of Trump's threats to resume attacks
articles.content_orig:
A source familiar with the ongoing diplomacy confirmed to CBS News that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday to convey the latest edits to a draft proposal to end the U.S. war with Iran.
The source said there were indications of progress being made.
A draft was presented by Qatari mediators last Sunday, and a response from Iran is expected by the weekend. The aim of the proposal is to avert a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which President Trump has threatened multiple times in recent weeks.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that two oil tankers had been halted after unspecified "incidents" as they attempted to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has repeatedly warned shippers that using the southern route through the waterway, which has been promoted by the U.S., puts them at risk as the regime deems it an illegal passage.
The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist U.S. military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route," the IRGC statement said.
The IRGC did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had been forced to stop in the area after hitting sea mines.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Qatari officials returned to Iran on Friday to push for a peace deal between Tehran and Washington, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency , along with Reuters and AFP, reported.
The talks have been coordinated with the U.S., an official told Reuters.
The delegation is led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister and is scheduled to meet with senior Iranian officials, IRNA said, adding that the discussions would focus on bilateral relations between Iran and Qatar, as well as developments in the region.
An official briefed on the latest diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , and that Tehran would not change its stance on the nuclear issue, something Washington wants included in negotiations from the start.
Tehran wants the U.S. to first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to drop sanctions limiting the country's gas and oil sales.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by President Trump but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
On Thursday, Mr. Trump said a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei — which was reported by multiple outlets as an attempt to restart peace negotiations — was an outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran has yet to reply to the letter, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.
Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.
Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.
The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations , which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it stopped using the name Operation Epic Fury for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reported.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
A tanker was struck Thursday evening by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center reported, after Iran's navy claimed four ships had struck sea mines in the area.
UKMTO said the ship hit by a projectile was exiting the strait along the southern route, which the U.S. has encouraged international shipping companies to use, when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," UKMTO said.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its military claimed in two separate announcements earlier Thursday that four tankers had struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires.
It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been struck by a projectile was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report from the maritime monitor suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
